Here's the full picture on your board feedback — **no existing cards covered it; two new ones are filed and on the board**:

**Your three observations, two root causes:**

1. **Hash-titled dispatch rows → [#75](https://github.com/polecatspeaks/StarCar/issues/75) (area:view).** The row title is the record-dir name, which is the dispatching agent's id hash. The human handle already exists in the store — the minted task-id like `view-69-71-car-r2` — it's just never surfaced. The card asks for task-id as title with an honest fallback to the hash when absent, hash retained as the provenance link. One nuance from decoding your screenshot: the `15:00` / `22:37` chips are #67's compact-clock *durations* (time since dispatch), not clock times — the two "dispatched" rows were this morning's two live dispatches (the r2 fix car and the friction miner), so that lane is live and honest, just unreadable as identity.

2. **Trains lane "old static info" + gates never populating → [#76](https://github.com/polecatspeaks/StarCar/issues/76) (area:tooling), one card because it's one defect.** Probed before filing: the store contains *zero* train manifests — the only train-scoped records are the v0 walking-skeleton intents from 07-23. Every real train since (#62, #65, #67, #69/#71) ran without minting one. **The #75 train is rolling** — Sonnet car dispatched in a fresh worktree cut from the green tip. Scope: thread the task-id through the full wire sentence (fold → wire → schema → render), title returned rows by their human task-id with an honest hash fallback, hash kept reachable via tooltip and provenance link, red-first at every hop including an asserting real-browser check. Hard scope boundary in the brief: the producer side (stamping task-id on *dispatched* records) stays untouched — that's #76's design territory, so in-flight rows keep showing hashes until then, which is honest.

When it returns: Opus adversarial review (the recordDir precedent's verdicts are the stated quality bar), then merge, close, board, restart.

While it runs, the one decision shaping the *next* train (#76): should train manifests be **minted whole at composition time** (the conductor knows the full member list when a train is planned — one record, but it goes stale if dispatch plans change mid-train) or **stamped incrementally by the producer as each dispatch launches** (always true, never stale, but the "planned vs actual" distinction is lost and the gates lane only fills as reviewers launch)? No rush — the car has a while to run — but your lean would let me draft #76's design with the premise settled rather than discovered in review.
why is the planned vs actual distinction lost? I think that's the more interesting question

Because under incremental stamping there's only one writer, and it's the launch event. Membership data then exists *only for launches that happened* — a planned car that never launched has no writer anywhere in the system. "Planned vs actual" needs two independent record streams: a plan written by the planner at composition, and actuals written as dispatches fire. Any design where the manifest is *derived from* the launches collapses the two by construction — the plan becomes, definitionally, whatever happened, which is another way of saying there is no plan on the record at all.

And you're right that it's the more interesting question, because chasing it reframes what the trains lane *is*. Two things fall out:

**First, it's our own scar wearing a new hat.** The #32 forensics found the producer hook silently skipped 2 of 3 dispatches, and the log's conclusion was: a dispatch that never writes its `dispatched` record isn't *overdue* — it's *invisible*, because the detector's input is produced by the same fallible layer it's supposed to check. Absence-blindness one layer down. A composition-time manifest is precisely the missing completeness assertion: once the plan says "this train has a car and a gate," a car that never launched becomes a *detectable absence* instead of a nothing. Incremental stamping can never give us that, no matter how reliable the stamping is, because it asserts nothing about what should exist.

**Second, it makes a currently trust-based shop rule observable.** "A car and its review are one unit" today binds only by conductor discipline — nothing on any surface shows a car that ran unreviewed. With role-carrying plan records, the board can render fulfillment state per member: planned → dispatched → returned, per role. A returned car whose paired gate is neither dispatched nor returned is a renderable FLAG, in exactly the register language the board already speaks. The gates lane stops being "empty until someone remembers to mint something" and becomes the review pipeline's promise-vs-delivery surface — which is about as StarCar as a feature can get.

So the composition-vs-incremental menu I offered was the wrong shape, and the stale-plan worry I attached to composition-time mostly dissolves on inspection: plans *do* change mid-train (a rotation adds a reviewer, a fix cycle adds rounds), but the store already has supersession semantics — an amended manifest supersedes its predecessor and the plan's own history stays legible, which is the metamorphism rule applied to plans. Fittingly, the walking skeleton's only train records were literally named `intent-*.json` — v0 already leaned this way and we didn't notice.

My revised recommendation for #76's design: **the manifest is a plan record, minted at composition, amended by supersession; dispatches are the actual stream; the board's product is the delta between them.** Incremental stamping can still exist later as corroboration, but it's enrichment, not the mechanism. Want me to write #76's design brief around that premise? It's grown past a coverage rider — this is a design-rung ticket now, and it'd go through the ladder.
yeah that seems to be the smarter and better way to go, update the ticket and lets run through the design while it's still early in the morning here
Updating the ticket with the ruling, then pulling the prior art and the real consumer contract so we design against code, not memory.

1	# Design document template
2	
3	Status: Current
4	Use: copy to `docs/design/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`.
5	
6	**Why this exists.** The ladder named design as rung 1 and gave it no artifact. Every other
7	rung had one - car brief, reviewer addendum, state ledger, gating matrix - and every other
8	rung worked. Design produced four REJECT rounds and twelve Majors on its first outing, and
9	the failures were not random: they landed exactly where the scaffolding was missing.
10	
11	The seed was ported from a shop where the design workflow was **tacit** - you do not need a
12	template when you can open last month's design and imitate it. The port carried the RULES
13	and not the EXEMPLARS. In a human shop that is survivable. Here it is fatal, because the
14	seed's own first premise is that every worker is a new hire on day one: **there is no last
15	month's design to open.**
16	
17	Rules tell you what is forbidden. Exemplars show you what compliance looks like. This file
18	is both.
19	
20	---
21	
22	## The order is the point
23	
24	Sections 0, 1 and 2 are written **before any mechanism exists**, and they are not
25	paperwork. They are the design equivalent of a red test: a constraint written down before
26	the thing it constrains, so that violating it is visible at construction time rather than
27	at review.
28	
29	**The tell that this was skipped:** the reviewer finds the law, not the author. In a
30	law-first process the author hits the constraint while writing and the reviewer finds
31	nothing there. If every constitution check in your review comes back with findings, the
32	constraints were not present when the mechanism was built.
33	
34	---
35	
36	## §0 - Instrument check (FIRST, and it can end the document)
37	
38	> **What kind of artifact is this?**
39	>
40	> - **Behavioural / architectural** - what should happen, which component owns what, how
41	>   failures surface. A reviewer can verify these by reading. **Prose design is correct.**
42	> - **Format, protocol, algorithm, wire contract** - canonicalisation, identity, ordering,
43	>   dedup, hashing, schema. **STOP. Prose cannot hold this.** Reviewing prose about a hash
44	>   function is reviewing a photograph of a machine. Go straight to an executable spec: a
45	>   schema file, conformance vectors, red-first tests. The artifact IS the precision.
46	> - **Both** - split the document. The behavioural half is prose; the precision half is a
47	>   pointer to the executable artifact and its tests.
48	
49	State the answer and the reason in one or two sentences. If the answer is "format", this
50	document should not be written.
51	
52	## §1 - Constraints (BEFORE the mechanism)
53	
54	> Which laws, templates, contracts and prior verdicts bind this design, and **what does
55	> each one FORBID**? Not a citation list - a list of prohibitions you are designing
56	> against.
57	
58	| Source | What it forbids here | How this design satisfies it |
59	|---|---|---|
60	| `constitution.md:N` Law N | *what it rules out* | *filled in as the mechanism is written* |
61	| `docs/templates/<x>.md` | | |
62	| a prior verdict in `artifacts/reviews/` | | |
63	
64	Open every source and quote the binding clause. A constraint you paraphrase from memory is
65	a constraint you will satisfy from memory.
66	
67	## §2 - Premises
68	
69	> What is being assumed that **no constraint forced**? List them plainly.
70	
71	Adversarial review is blind to unquestioned premises: a reviewer rejects what is on the
72	page, and cannot reject the assumption that put it there. A premise written down is a
73	premise that can be attacked. A premise left implicit will survive every round of review
74	and will be the thing that was actually wrong.
75	
76	For each: **what would change if it were false?** If the answer is "most of this document,"
77	that premise deserves its own scrutiny before anything else is written.
78	
79	## §2c - Probe list (what the desk CANNOT prove)
80	
81	> Everything this design assumes but **cannot verify from here**. Not premises you chose -
82	> facts you could not check. Each with what would settle it.
83	
84	| Claim | Why unverifiable from the desk | What would settle it |
85	|---|---|---|
86	
87	Borrowed from the ancestor shop's spec shape, where it is a mandatory section. The rule
88	that makes it work: **an unverifiable claim goes HERE explicitly - never assumed into the
89	mechanism.** A probe item is honest; the same claim stated as fact in §5 is a defect

93	branch its negative result takes.

102	
103	| # | Decision | Reason | Which constraint or premise drove it |
104	|---|---|---|---|
105	
106	The last column is load-bearing: a decision that traces to neither a constraint nor a

108	
109	## §5 - Mechanism
110	
111	The design proper. Types, flows, components, interfaces.

114	
115	Every way it breaks, what the system does, and which law that behaviour honours. Absence,
116	staleness, partial data, conflicting sources, and the unknown state - `constitution.md:17`

118

138	|---|---|---|---|
139	| Major 1 … | finding | adopted | §5.3 |
140	| Ruling on Q1 … | **ruling** | appealed - reason, evidence | §4 |

143	An implementer never silently overrides its own reviewer; rejection is appealable upward,
144	never around. Disagreeing is legitimate and welcome - **disagreeing quietly is not**, and
145	the failure mode is never a loud argument, it is an item that simply stops appearing.
146	
147	This is a structural guard against a known model bias, not a discipline exercise. A pull
148	toward smoothing over conflict is not something an author can decide not to have; a table
149	with an empty cell in it is something a reviewer can see.

content.text:
The prior art changes the design's size — most of the machine already exists, landed and tested from the v0 spec:

**What's already true:** a manifest is an `intent`-kind record, subject `train:<id>` (partition rule, ruled at Q7), payload `{title, tickets, members[{subject, role, gate?}]}`. Supersession (winning-manifest-per-train) is implemented with a conformance vector. Assemble already handles `declared-not-observed` members, manifest collisions, unreadable payloads. And a ruling that matters to us: **D16 — membership and roles are conductor-declared originals; status never flows from a manifest.** Fulfillment is the fold's join, never a plan field. That ruling is exactly the plan-vs-actual premise, already carved into the schema's description.

**Why it's never populated:** the v0 manifests were minted *retroactively* — `members[].subject` is required and is the *dispatch id*, which only exists after launch. And the v0 members used role `reviewer`, while the gates lane keys on role `gate` — so even the one manifest that exists feeds no gates. Both facts point at the same four decisions, which are the whole design:

**D1 — member identity at plan time.** Members need a key the conductor knows at composition. That's the minted task-id (`view-75-car-r1`), which the envelope already echoes into returned records and #75 is threading to the wire right now. Proposal: members declare `task_id` + `role` (+ `gate`); `subject` becomes optional-at-declaration. My lean is firm here — it's the only key that exists before launch.

**D2 — when the agent id attaches.** Two honest options: **(a)** the conductor amends the manifest at each dispatch (I know the agent id the moment I spawn it) — one superseding record per launch, board joins in-flight rows immediately; **(b)** no amendment — the join happens at return via the task-id echo, zero mid-train minting, but in-flight dispatches sit unjoined and plan members read "declared, not observed" *while their car is actually running*, which is a false-ish surface during the run. I lean **(a)**: the board is live and honest mid-train, and the amendment is one scripted command that tooling can make near-free.

**D3 — roles vocabulary.** The ladder's per-car adversarial reviewers *are* gates. Proposal: they get role `gate` with a gate name (`car-review r2`), reserving `reviewer` as legacy vocab; roles live in `schema/vocab/roles.json` as data (Law 7), so this is a vocab-and-doctrine decision, not code. Alternative: teach assemble to treat `reviewer` as gate-ish — but that's semantics in code, which Law 7 frowns at.

**D4 — the fulfillment states and the unit-rule FLAG.** Per-member: declared → dispatched → returned-with-outcome (verdict word verbatim in the gates lane), plus presumed-lost. And the piece you liked: a returned `car` member with no paired `gate` member dispatched-or-returned renders as a FLAG-tier condition — the car-and-review unit rule made observable. Needs a pairing convention (member order vs explicit reference); my lean is explicit (`for: <task_id>` on the gate member) — order is a silent convention, and silent conventions are how nine wire fields die.

Terminal/archival state stays out of scope (#68 owns retrieval; a train with all members returned simply reads complete).

If your leans match — task-id members, amend-at-dispatch, gate role with names, explicit pairing — I'll write the design doc law-first against D16/DR3-1/DR3-3/SB-1 and the v0 verdicts, with a probe list (first probe: mint a hand-made plan manifest into a scratch store and see what today's assemble actually renders — the declared-not-observed path may already do half of D4). Where do you land on D2 especially? It's the one with a real cost trade (a superseding record per dispatch vs a quiet board mid-train).
errm. yeah ok, that seems more sane. send it.

Taking "send it" as ruling all four leans as stated — task-id members, amend-at-dispatch, `gate` role with names, explicit pairing. Probing before writing, per doctrine: what does today's assemble actually render for a plan-shaped manifest?

`declaredNotObserved` already renders — part of D4 exists. Now the decisive behavioural probe: does today's code fill the **gates lane** from a `gate`-role member? Checking how the server takes a store path, then running it.

**Stop the design — the probe killed most of it, and that's the best outcome available.** I built a plan-shaped manifest in a scratch store and pointed the real board server at it. Everything we were about to design already exists and works:

- **The gates lane filled**: `{"name":"car-review r1","subject":"gateA","outcome":"APPROVE",...}` — verdict word carried, from a `gate`-role member.
- **The trains lane rendered the full consist** with per-member role, state, outcome, and provenance.
- **`declaredNotObserved: ["gateB"]`** — the member I declared and never launched came back as a *named absence*. The completeness assertion we reasoned our way to this morning is already built.
- Every member record came back `assigned: true`, so the "92 unassigned" symptom resolves too. Zero board conditions raised.

So all three of your observations have one cause, and it isn't missing board code: **nobody mints manifests.** The v0 walking-skeleton ones were minted retroactively and used role `reviewer` where the gates lane keys on `gate` — which is why the one manifest that exists feeds nothing.

What's genuinely left is narrow, and my four "decisions" mostly evaporated: roles-as-data, supersession, collision detection, unreadable-payload disclosure — all landed and tested. The real remainder is (1) **plan-time member identity** — the schema requires a member's `subject`, which *is* the dispatch id and doesn't exist at composition; a placeholder stays `declaredNotObserved` forever while the real dispatch lands as unassigned, so one miss produces two wrong surfaces. That's D1/D2 and it's still a live question, now sharpened by #75's task-id work being in flight. (2) The **unit-rule FLAG** — genuinely new, needs explicit pairing on the member. (3) The **minting mechanism** itself.

That's not a design-rung train anymore; it's one narrow identity ruling plus tooling. The probe cost about four minutes and is recorded on #76 with the rebuild recipe. My own premise — "the board can't do this yet" — was simply false, and I'd have written a design specifying mechanisms that already exist.

Recommendation: don't write the design doc.
